message:
The main headline on Sunday is strong winds. This would usually be a problem, but the mountains along the Continental Divide which have the strongest winds have the least snow. The exception is the Zirkel Wilderness and the Mosquito Range, but even there, avalanche-producing slopes are rare.

The main thing to watch for right now is small, recent wind drifts on northerly-facing slopes above about 12,000 feet. Strong southwest winds have transported the new snow, loading terrain features where the underlying snowpack is weakest. Southwest winds are particularly concerning because they load some of the same terrain features where the existing snow is most faceted. Finding the right combination of connected terrain, wind-drifted snow, and old snow underneath will be difficult, but it isn't impossible.

The pattern of small storms delivering very little snow will continue on Monday. We don’t expect the avalanche danger to increase through at least Thanksgiving. Although avalanche concerns are minimal right now, these small storms are gradually adding to the snow cover, while the breaks between storms are promoting faceting of the existing snowpack. We may not be dealing with meaningful avalanche problems right now, but the snowpack is slowly becoming more developed and weaker. When the first major storm cycle arrives, avalanche danger could rise quickly.

Images.caption: Looking west from the top of Loveland Pass on November 15. You can see there isn't quite enough snow to overcome surface roughness on these north-, northeast-, and east-facing slopes, but maybe enough to form a weak layer in the future.
Images.altText: A rounded alpine ridge with patchy snow cover

Images.caption: The north-facing slopes of Red Peak from Hoosier Pass on November 12. This is one of the snowier areas in the Northern Mountains right now.
Drifts of firm snow like this are areas to be cautious. Imagine sliding into the sharp rocks below.
Images.altText: Sunlit evergreen branches in the lower left foreground overlook a shaded, wind-rippled snow slope descending toward a dark treeline, with a sunlit, pine-dotted mountainside rising across the valley.

Images.caption: Weak grains like this depth hoar found at Guanella Pass will be problematic once we get a large storm.
Images.altText: Close-up of angular, translucent faceted ice crystals arranged in three vertical clusters on a black surface.

message:
A bit more snow fell than expected across the West Elk Mountains through the Elk Mountains over to Independence Pass Friday through Saturday, bringing around 8 to 12 inches of new snow. This new snow, combined with the last two small storms that brought few inches each. We now have a cohesive slab across upper elevation slopes sitting on a persistent weak layer from the early November dry spell on most slopes facing the north half of the compass, generally above around 10,500 to 11,000 feet.

Numerous avalanches were remotely triggered across the Elk Mountains and Independence Pass on Saturday above 11,000 feet, and conditions won’t dramatically improve overnight. The most dangerous areas are where wind drifted additional snow, so slabs are both thicker and firmer, meaning they will break wider and grow larger than you might expect. Some of these avalanches were triggered from hundreds of feet away and were close calls for some backcountry travelers.

Another small storm looks like it could impact the area again Monday afternoon. This storm looks smaller than the last few, but that could change, and even just a few more inches added on to this already existing slab could easily keep the danger elevated through much of Thanksgiving week.

There is not as much concern where not enough snow fell the last two days to develop a slab, or where the new snow fell on bare ground or a crust. That means most slopes below 10,000 feet and most south-facing slopes are far less concerning and unlikely to trigger a dangerous avalanche.

Images.caption: This avalanche was triggered from around 300 feet away on a northeast-facing slope near treeline in Yule Creek, between Marble and Crested Butte on Saturday, November 21, 2026.
Images.altText: Looking across a snowy slope at an avalanche.

message:
More snow at the tail end of the storm and wider avalanches than expected on Saturday has us raising the danger to Considerable (3 of 5) for Sunday.  Most areas received 4 to 6 inches of snow, while others, like Lone Cone and the northwest corner of the San Juans, picked up as much as 10 inches. The final pulse of snowfall came in with lighter winds and colder temperatures, meaning there is a low-density layer of fluff covering up the drifted areas formed by strong winds at the start of the storm. With surface clues obscured by the new snow, it all comes down to managing your terrain choices in order to avoid avalanches this weekend. Leeward slopes below ridgelines facing north and northeast have been the bullseye for reactivity and are places to avoid on Sunday.  

Strong winds earlier in the week, on Tuesday, brought an abrupt change to our snowpack, finally forming slabs in wind-drifted areas over a widespread weak layer that formed during the early-November dryspell. In the days since that wind event, we’ve recorded 28 avalanches, 14 of which were human-triggered, and one that caught someone. With strong southerly winds driving snow transport and slab formation, the most dangerous areas have been north and northeast-facing slopes above treeline. 

This avalanche on Trico Peak is a good illustration of the wind-drifted slopes we’re most worried about. The larger avalanche on the right was triggered by the first skier as they descended, but the smaller slides to the left were remote-triggered above them as they traversed across the slope. This means we need to give wide margins to steep overhead slopes as we now have the potential to trigger avalanches from below or from a distance. The reactive nature of the weak layer that was buried on November 14th means that Persistent Slab avalanches are here and will stay on the menu for the foreseeable future. 

After an especially deep and stable start to the season, our snowpack is evolving and becoming more dangerous. Choose your slopes carefully this weekend and assess the snowpack for a slab over weak layer setup before engaging with terrain steeper than 35 degrees. You can always find safer travel in wind-sheltered trees.

Images.caption: Following strong winds and modest snowfall on November 17th, we saw our first rash of human-triggered Persistent Slab avalanches. Some were remotely-triggered and one even temporarily caught a skier.

Winds on November 17th dramatically changed the snowpack and avalanche conditions by forming a reactive slab over weak snow across upper elevation terrain. Another wind event overnight and into November 20th continues to press and stiffen alpine snow surfaces.

There have been more human-triggered avalanches in the past week than at any point this season. They are also becoming larger in size. This screenshot from our Avalanche Explorer Map shows a key takeaway: 75% of avalanches happened on north and northeast-facing slopes above treeline. Factor this knowledge into your tour planning process and choose different aspects or less-steep slopes.
